title: Filesystem map
description: Explore the standard Linux directories, from `/bin` to `/var/tmp`: what lives where, an example from the TuxPixel machine, and which ones are pseudo filesystems.
intro: Open `/proc`, then `/sys` and `/dev`, and read where their data is stored: none of it is on disk. Next, compare `/tmp` with `/var/tmp`, then `/bin` with `/usr/bin`. Finally, answer the "where would you look?" questions without peeking at the map.
takeaways: `/etc` holds system-wide configuration files; `/home` holds users' files (`~` is yours, and `/root` is the administrator's home); `/var/log` holds plain-text logs; `/boot` holds the kernel and boot files.

Commands live in `/bin` and `/usr/bin` (for all users) and in `/sbin` and `/usr/sbin` (administration). On current Debian, `/bin` and `/sbin` are symbolic links to `/usr/bin` and `/usr/sbin`, which is why a listing of both looks the same.

`/proc` (processes and kernel information), `/sys` (devices and drivers) and `/dev` (device files) are made by the kernel while the system runs. They take no disk space: what you read is produced by the kernel at that moment.

`/tmp` is for throw-away files, and nothing you put there should be relied on after a reboot. `/var/tmp` is meant for temporary files that stay across reboots. Both are writable by everyone and carry the sticky bit.
`/usr/share/doc/<package>/` holds the extra documentation packages install, such as README files and changelogs; man pages are elsewhere (`/usr/share/man`).
`/` is the top of the tree, `/root` is the administrator's home and `/home` holds everyone else's. Mixing up `/` and `/root` is a classic mistake.

directories.role: The root of the whole tree
directories.contents: Every file and directory on the machine lives somewhere below `/`. The top level holds the main directories on this map. Do not confuse `/` with `/root`, the home directory of the administrator.
directories.storageNote: The root filesystem is on disk; other filesystems (and the pseudo ones below) are attached to directories under it.
directories.atTuxPixel: Mira starts any absolute path with `/`, such as `/etc/hostname`, and it means the same thing from every directory.
directories.examTip: `/` is the top of the tree and `/root` is a home directory. They are different things.

directories.contents: The programs everyone needs, even for repairs: `ls`, `cp`, `cat`, `bash`.
directories.storageNote: Real programs stored on disk.
directories.atTuxPixel: When Ada types `ls`, the shell finds it through `PATH`, on a modern Debian under `/usr/bin` as well as `/bin`.
directories.examTip: Traditionally `/bin` holds the essential user commands. On current Debian it is a symbolic link to `/usr/bin`, so both paths show the same programs.

directories.role: Files the machine needs to start
directories.contents: The Linux kernel image (`vmlinuz-…`), the initial RAM disk (`initrd.img-…`) and boot loader files.
directories.storageNote: Ordinary files on disk, often on a small partition of their own.
directories.atTuxPixel: Before Mira reboots the build server after an update, she can check that a new `vmlinuz` appeared here.
directories.examTip: `/boot` is where the kernel image lives. Together with `/dev` and `/sys` it is a hardware-related path in objective 014.2.

directories.contents: Files that stand for hardware and pseudo-devices: disks (`/dev/sda`), terminals, and special ones such as `/dev/null`, `/dev/zero` and `/dev/urandom`.
directories.storageNote: The kernel and udev create the entries while the system runs (type `devtmpfs`); nothing is stored on disk.
directories.atTuxPixel: Jonas sends noisy build messages to `/dev/null`; Ada reads random bytes from `/dev/urandom` for a test key.
directories.examTip: Disks are block devices (`b` in `ls -l`), and `/dev/null` and terminals are character devices (`c`). `/dev` is a special kernel-managed directory, not ordinary storage.

directories.contents: Plain-text configuration files for the system and its services, such as `hostname`, `passwd`, `hosts` and `fstab`.
directories.storageNote: Ordinary files on disk. Programs read them; the administrator edits them.
directories.atTuxPixel: Mira checks `/etc/hostname` to confirm that the guest machine is called `tuxpixel`.
directories.examTip: Settings for the whole machine live in `/etc`; one user's own settings live in hidden files in that user's home directory.

directories.contents: One directory per user, such as `/home/mira`, for personal files and settings. The shell writes `~` for your own.
directories.storageNote: Ordinary files on disk, often on a separate partition so reinstalling the system keeps them.
directories.atTuxPixel: Jonas keeps his sprite files under `/home/jonas`; Ada has `/home/ada`.
directories.examTip: `~` stands for your home directory, `~jonas` for Jonas's. The administrator's home is `/root`, not under `/home`.

directories.contents: Code that programs share, and the kernel modules under `/lib/modules`.
directories.storageNote: Real files on disk.
directories.atTuxPixel: The loadable driver modules of the guest's kernel are in a folder named after the kernel version.
directories.examTip: Libraries are shared code that programs load. Like `/bin`, `/lib` is a link to `/usr/lib` on current Debian.

directories.role: Processes and kernel data as files
directories.contents: A folder per running process, named by its PID (`/proc/1234/`), plus system facts such as `/proc/cpuinfo` and `/proc/meminfo`.
directories.storageNote: A pseudo filesystem (type `proc`): the kernel makes the content up when you read it, and nothing is on disk.
directories.atTuxPixel: When Ada wonders what a stuck program is, `/proc/<PID>/` tells her. On this machine, process 1 is `le-init`; on a normal Debian it is `systemd`.
directories.examTip: `/proc` is a pseudo filesystem. Its files look like text files but report the live state of processes and the kernel.

directories.contents: Personal files of the `root` user. Ordinary users cannot enter it.
directories.storageNote: Ordinary files on disk.
directories.atTuxPixel: Mira does not work as root; she uses `sudo` and her own `/home/mira`.
directories.examTip: `/root` is not `/`. It is root's home directory, outside `/home` and closed to everyone else.

directories.contents: Small runtime files made since the last boot: PID files, sockets and lock files.
directories.storageNote: A tmpfs (a filesystem in memory), so it starts empty at every boot.
directories.atTuxPixel: Services started on a machine write their PID and socket files here.
directories.examTip: `/run` is runtime data in memory; it is rebuilt at every boot and not meant for your files.

directories.contents: Programs for the administrator, such as `fsck` and `reboot`.
directories.storageNote: Real programs stored on disk.
directories.atTuxPixel: Mira uses `sudo` to run tools from here and from `/usr/sbin`.
directories.examTip: `/sbin` and `/usr/sbin` hold administration programs. On current Debian `/sbin` is a link to `/usr/sbin`.

directories.contents: The kernel's view of hardware, drivers and buses: `/sys/class/net/` for network interfaces, `/sys/block/` for disks.
directories.storageNote: A pseudo filesystem (type `sysfs`) made by the kernel; nothing is stored on disk.
directories.atTuxPixel: Ada lists `/sys/class/net` to see which network interfaces a machine has. The browser guest shows only the loopback interface `lo`.
directories.examTip: `/sys` is a pseudo filesystem like `/proc`, but about devices and drivers rather than processes.

directories.contents: Scratch files that programs and users make and that may disappear at any time.
directories.storageNote: Distributions either clean it at boot (when it lives on disk) or mount it as a tmpfs in memory. On the guest it is a tmpfs.
directories.atTuxPixel: Jonas exports a quick preview there. If he needs it tomorrow, he moves it out.
directories.examTip: Everyone can write to `/tmp`, and the sticky bit (`t`) stops users deleting each other's files. Do not rely on its content surviving a reboot.

directories.contents: The big section for installed software: `bin`, `sbin`, `lib`, `share`, `local` and more.
directories.storageNote: Real files on disk, changed only when software is installed or updated.
directories.atTuxPixel: Almost every program Mira runs, from `tar` to `grep`, is under `/usr`.
directories.examTip: `/usr` is not user data and not the home directories; it is where installed software lives.

directories.contents: The commands you type every day: `tar`, `gzip`, `grep`, `find`.
directories.storageNote: Real programs stored on disk.
directories.atTuxPixel: This is where `tar` and `gzip` live, for the assets archive.
directories.examTip: Normal commands for all users are in `/usr/bin` (and `/bin`). Both are normally in your `PATH`.

directories.contents: Tools for managing the machine, such as `useradd`, `adduser` and `groupadd`, mainly meant for root.
directories.storageNote: Real programs stored on disk.
directories.atTuxPixel: Mira runs `sudo useradd` to add a user; the program is here.
directories.examTip: Administration programs are in `/usr/sbin` and `/sbin`. An ordinary user's `PATH` usually does not list them, as the output of `echo $PATH` shows.

directories.contents: Files that work the same on any processor type: documentation (`doc`), manual pages (`man`), icons, locale data and more.
directories.storageNote: Real files on disk.
directories.atTuxPixel: The man pages Mira reads and the documentation Ada looks up both come from here.
directories.examTip: Documentation is under `/usr/share`: manual pages in `man`, other package documentation in `doc`.

directories.contents: One folder per installed package with its README, changelog, copyright notice and example files.
directories.storageNote: Ordinary files on disk.
directories.atTuxPixel: Before configuring a tool, Mira looks here for the package's examples.
directories.examTip: Besides man pages, packages install extra documentation under `/usr/share/doc/<package>/`.

directories.role: Data that changes while the system runs
directories.contents: Logs, caches, mail and print queues, package databases and other files that grow and change.
directories.storageNote: Ordinary files on disk, often on its own partition so a runaway log cannot fill the root filesystem.
directories.atTuxPixel: The game server's logs and caches pile up here.
directories.examTip: `/var` is for variable data. The two parts you must know are `/var/log` and `/var/tmp`.

directories.contents: Plain-text logs written by the system and services, such as `dpkg.log` and, on many systems, `syslog` or `auth.log`.
directories.storageNote: Ordinary files on disk. Logrotate renames and compresses old ones.
directories.atTuxPixel: Ada reads the build daemon's log here with `tail` or `less`.
directories.examTip: Most plain-text log files are under `/var/log`. On systemd machines the journal holds more, read with `journalctl`.

directories.role: Temporary files that survive a reboot
directories.contents: Scratch files that must stay available after the machine restarts.
directories.storageNote: Kept on disk, and not cleaned at boot.
directories.atTuxPixel: Jonas parks a half-finished export here when it must still be there after Mira reboots the server.
directories.examTip: Compare `/tmp` and `/var/tmp`: both are world-writable with the sticky bit, but only `/var/tmp` is meant to keep files across reboots. (`9p` is how this browser guest attaches its disk.)

quiz.text: Mira wants to change which name the machine calls itself. Where is the setting file?
quiz.why: System-wide settings are text files in `/etc`; here it is `/etc/hostname`.

quiz.text: Ada wants to see which processes are running by looking at files, one folder per process ID.
quiz.why: Each process has a folder `/proc/<PID>/`, filled in by the kernel.

quiz.text: Jonas wants the plain-text log that the build daemon wrote yesterday.
quiz.why: Services write their text logs under `/var/log`.

quiz.text: Mira needs the Linux kernel image the machine boots from.
quiz.why: The kernel (`vmlinuz-…`) and the initial RAM disk are in `/boot`.

quiz.text: Jonas wants a scratch folder for a preview that can vanish at the next reboot.
quiz.why: `/tmp` is for short-lived files that may be cleaned or lost at a reboot. `/var/tmp` is for files that must survive one.

quiz.text: Ada's test export has to survive the server's nightly reboot, so she wants a temporary place that is kept.
quiz.why: Only `/var/tmp` is meant to keep its files across reboots.

quiz.text: Mira wants the device file for the first SATA disk.
quiz.why: Disks are device files such as `/dev/sda`, made by the kernel in `/dev`.

quiz.text: Where does Jonas keep his personal sprite files?
quiz.why: Every ordinary user has a home directory under `/home`, such as `/home/jonas`.

quiz.text: Mira asks where the programs `ls` and `cp` are stored on a current Debian machine.
quiz.why: Everyday commands are in `/usr/bin` (and `/bin`, which links to it).

quiz.text: Ada wants the README and changelog that came with an installed package.
Where would Mira find `useradd`, a tool for creating users?
Ada wants to know which network interfaces the kernel found, by looking at files about hardware and drivers.
quiz.why: `/sys/class/net/` lists the network interfaces. `/sys` shows devices and drivers.
